facts.summary: Wyoming has no state daily-overtime or higher salary threshold; the federal FLSA standard (1.5x after 40 hrs/week) applies.
facts.sourceAgency: Wyoming Dept of Workforce Services, Labor Standards
facts.notes: Confirm no state OT overlay on the DWS Labor Standards page.

facts.summary: Wyoming's statutory minimum wage is $5.15, but the federal $7.25 applies to employees covered by the FLSA, so $7.25 is effective for most workers.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Dept of Labor (state minimum-wage table)
facts.notes: Wyoming's own $5.15 figure is preempted by federal for FLSA-covered employers; verify on DWS.

value: and the federal classes (via the Wyoming Fair Employment Practices Act)
facts.summary: The Wyoming Fair Employment Practices Act prohibits discrimination on the federal bases and is enforced by the Wyoming Dept of Workforce Services.
facts.notes: Verify the exact protected-class list and any state additions on the DWS page.

facts.summary: The Wyoming Fair Employment Practices Act applies to employers with two or more employees — broader than the federal 15-employee threshold.
facts.notes: VERIFY employee-count threshold against the statute.

facts.value: 2 years (3 if willful) under FLSA; 8 years under Wyoming's general statutory-liability limitation
facts.summary: A claim brought under the federal FLSA follows the federal 2-year (3-year if willful) limit; a Wyoming state-law wage claim (e.g., under the Wyoming wage-payment statute) is not FLSA-limited and instead falls under Wyoming's general 8-year period for 'a liability created by statute.'
facts.citation: 29 U.S.C. § 255(a) (federal FLSA claims); Wyo. Stat. § 1-3-105(a)(ii)(B) (state statutory-liability claims)
facts.notes: CORRECTED: this fact previously cited Wyo. Stat. § 27-4-104 as the source of the state limitations period, but that section (confirmed directly against primary text) does not set a statute of limitations at all -- it governs final-pay timing and an 18%/year interest penalty for late payment (see the new final-pay fact, below). Wyoming's Title 27 sets no dedicated wage-claim limitations period, so the general 8-year 'liability created by statute' period in § 1-3-105(a)(ii)(B) (confirmed directly against primary text) is the state-law period understood to apply, distinct from and longer than the federal FLSA period.

facts.value: next regular scheduled payday (discharge or quit)
facts.summary: Whether an employee quits or is discharged, Wyoming requires payment of wages due no later than the employer's usual practice on regularly scheduled payroll dates (or as set by a collective bargaining agreement); Wyoming does not require accelerated/immediate payment the way some states do.
facts.notes: Confirmed directly against primary statute text. Subsection (b) entitles an employee who sues for unpaid wages to 18% annual interest on the past-due amount from the date of discharge/termination, plus reasonable attorney fees and costs; § 27-4-105 separately makes willful nonpayment a civil penalty.

facts.summary: Wyoming's Occupational Health and Safety Act bars an employer from discharging or discriminating against an employee for filing a complaint, instituting or testifying in a related proceeding, or exercising any right afforded by the Act, whether on the employee's own behalf or another's.
facts.notes: Confirmed directly against primary statute text. Wyoming has no single broad private-sector whistleblower statute; this OSHA-related provision is the general-purpose one. Separately, public employees are protected from retaliation for reporting fraud, waste, or health/safety risks under Wyo. Stat. § 9-11-102 et seq., and narrower sector-specific protections exist (e.g., health-care-facility employees under § 35-2-910(b), long-term-care ombudsman reports under § 9-2-1308, wage-discrimination retaliation under § 27-4-304) -- none of those were independently verified against primary text this session.

facts.summary: A discrimination or unfair-employment-practice complaint must be filed with the Department of Workforce Services within six months of the alleged violation.
facts.notes: Confirmed directly against primary statute text. Substantially shorter than the federal EEOC 180/300-day deadlines, so a worker with a federally-covered claim should also consider filing directly with the EEOC within the federal window.
